passages.title: Water Reuse in Modern Cities
passages.intro: An academic-style overview of environment, examining evidence and practical implications.
paras: Properly treated wastewater can be reused for purposes such as irrigation. The required treatment level depends on how the water will be used.
Public acceptance is influenced by trust in institutions and clear information. Some reuse systems require separate plumbing networks.
Different treatment methods consume different amounts of energy. Regular monitoring can identify problems before they become serious.
Reusing water can reduce demand on rivers, lakes and groundwater. Successful systems require plans for ongoing operation and maintenance.

paras: Street trees shade pavements and people walking beneath them. Tree species should suit the local climate, soil and available space.

Some neighbourhoods have much more tree canopy than others. A varied mix of species may reduce the risk that one pest harms the entire urban forest.
Many tree benefits grow as trees develop larger canopies. Urban tree programmes work better when maintenance responsibility is defined.

passages.title: Why Languages Borrow Words
passages.intro: An academic-style overview of linguistics, examining evidence and practical implications.
paras: Trade brings speakers of different languages into regular contact. A borrowed word often adapts to the sounds of the receiving language.
Languages may borrow words for objects or practices that were previously unfamiliar. A borrowed term may coexist with an older native word.
Words from a socially prestigious language may be adopted more readily. The meaning of a borrowed word may change in its new linguistic setting.
Dictionaries document patterns of use, although they can also influence them. Online communication creates new opportunities for words to cross language boundaries.
